extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary theory, poets and creative writers studying Aristotelian poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles drawn from an academic account of Aristotle's Poetics about how poetry and fine art should represent human life, structure events, and achieve poetic truth. Useful for writers and critics applying Aristotelian standards to composition and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation expresses the universal
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitative art (especially poetry) is an expression of the universal element in human life; fine art eliminates what is transient and particular and reveals the permanent and essential features (the εἶδος) of the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art discovers the 'form' towards which objects tend; the artist should aim to represent what is essential and universal beneath individual particulars rather than merely copying surface facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art aims at τὸ βέλτιον (the better / ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist produces a βέλτιον—a 'better' or higher reality—not merely a copy of actual experience; the ideal type must surpass the actual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take 'the better' in an aesthetic (not moral) sense: the work should present a purified, improved version of reality that reveals the ideal intentions of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine art idealizes and completes nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine art completes or 'carries forward' nature's movement toward an end by presenting a purified image that removes the flaws and failures of natural processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fine art need not reproduce the slow, halting steps of natural development; it may present the end-state or perfected form, revealing nature's aim rather than practical function (distinguishing fine art from useful art).

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony and unity of type
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist must harmonise selected elements into an ideal unity of type; mere selection, combination, embellishment or servile copying is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond choosing and embellishing beautiful parts, the work must stamp the given material with the impress of the universal form so that the parts cohere into a unified whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as creative, not servile
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation is a creative act: to seize the universal and reproduce it in simple, sensuous form; art is a rivalry of nature and a correction or completion of her failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat imitation as producing according to a 'true idea'—the artist invents and realises the ideal implicit in particulars rather than merely reflecting appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter: the possible (what may happen)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry relates what may happen—what is possible according to the law of probability or necessity—rather than merely recording what has happened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subject-matter that expresses τὰ καθόλου (the general/universal) and the permanent possibilities of human nature (οἷα ἂν γένοιτο), rather than only particular historical facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous causal connexion and internal cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem (especially tragedy) must exhibit a rigorous connection of events: cause and event should be linked in probable or necessary sequence; the inner law secures cohesion of parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot and character development should demonstrate internal necessity or likelihood (κατὰ τὸ εἰκὸς ἢ τὸ ἀναγκαῖον), not merely chronological ordering of incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability judged by internal plausibility, not statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: The εἰκός (probable) in poetry is not empirical frequency but what is fitting or likely within the poet's invented world and given character types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not measure poetic probability by common occurrence; judge it by whether actions and events follow plausibly from the nature and stature of the characters and the internal logic of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters as embodiments of the universal
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should represent the universal features of human nature—often not 'average' people but fuller types (e.g., Prometheus, Clytemnestra) whose deeds and passions reveal general truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Idealise characters so their inner necessity and responses illuminate universal human capacities; the reader's sympathy enlarges their own nature in response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor factual or technical errors are tolerable
rubrics_metrics.description: Small oversights, inconsistencies, or technical inaccuracies are not serious flaws provided they leave the total poetic impression unimpaired; distinguish errors affecting the essence of art from mere factual errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise total effect and unity; fix factual errors only insofar as they harm the work's essential integrity and plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth (the 'ought to be') over literal fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic truth differs from factual truth: poetry presents 'a higher reality' (ἀλλὰ βέλτιον), the form of what ought to be rather than a record of empirical events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for imaginative or moral truth that reveals essential patterns, even when the literal events depicted never happened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of an initial fictional premise (πρῶτον ψεῦδος) responsibly
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may posit a primary falsehood or set of imaginative assumptions, and then must make subsequent events follow plausibly from those premises so that the fiction yields believable effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a consistent imaginative environment; intense vividness, minute detail, and natural motive-sequence will make the fiction convincing and prevent the audience from being 'dashed against' prosaic reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'probable impossibilities' to 'improbable possibilities'
rubrics_metrics.description: Events impossible in fact may be preferable if the art makes them appear probable; such 'probable impossibilities' serve poetic ends better than unlikely but technically possible incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding on incidents, favour those that can be rendered internally inevitable by artistic treatment even if empirically impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid irrational (ἄλογα) elements unless justified by effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrational elements that provoke logical rejection are dangerous; they can be admitted only when specially justified—e.g., in epic for heightened wonder and admiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include events that violate internal causality unless the resultant effect (wonder, awe) justifies the breach and does not break the audience's imaginative assent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform and purify traditional/historical material
rubrics_metrics.description: Legends, myths, and historical incidents are valuable raw material but require the artist's shaping activity: extraction of the poetical ore, purification from the accidental and irrelevant, and idealisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tradition as a storehouse of material but subject it to selection, purification, and recomposition so that it attains unity and poetic truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit intervening natural steps; present the perfected form
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist may ignore the intervening steps of nature and present the completed ideal (the end) concretely; art reveals the ideal without dwelling on the slow processes nature uses to reach it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus representation on the essential completed form and the revealing moments; do not feel compelled to narrate every transitional or prosaic step that occurs in natural development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as a regulative principle (but not sole end)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle treats beauty as indispensable in a work of art and essential to achieving art's end, though he does not analyze beauty as a separate domain or claim that manifesting beauty is the sole end of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for beauty as a guiding principle—order, proportion, and fittingness—while recognising that the highest aims of art include revelation of universal truth and unity, not beauty alone.
